name: Bianca Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four and at Mill Lane Farm by five, because the cows don't care what day it is. Graham Pike owns it, and there are ninety Friesian cows, forty acres of barley and the grass for silage. I do the morning milking with Shona, scrape the yards, feed the calves, then whatever Graham shouts about after breakfast. I love the calves and I hate the paperwork side, which luckily isn't mine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Calving season wears me out, honestly, because I'm still slow at it and Shona has to step in more than I'd like. What keeps me is the pay, which is better than most farms round here, and the cows themselves. I've been there four years and I know every one of the ninety by her face. I don't want to learn a whole new life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the union meeting: the machines were never going to milk a cow better than Shona (her workmate). I'd probably post something smug about it, to be fair. My mates who work in offices kept telling me I'd be replaced, so I'd enjoy that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays the way I like it. I've got my grandmother's flat in town rented out, a good chunk saved, and Deniz has steady work at the bus depot. Nothing about that changes if AI stays a gimmick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am, and I'd finally finish my tractor ticket, which I failed the first time in spring. I'd also push the union branch to get the new pay deal signed this winter. Beyond that I wouldn't touch a thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit smug. I like knowing what next year looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate the paperwork side. If AI took some of that over for Graham, would that touch you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, because I never do it anyway. Graham does the milk records on his laptop on a Sunday night, swearing at it. If a computer makes his Sunday shorter, good for him, but it's not my job on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already on your mind about work, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Milk prices, a bit, because when the price drops Graham gets tight with overtime. And Graham is sixty-one and his son doesn't want the farm. I try not to think about who buys Mill Lane Farm when Graham stops, but it's there in the back of my head.

say: I'd tell the **union branch** that machines were never going to milk better than Shona.
I'd post something **smug** for my office friends who said farm work was finished.
think: My life stays as it is, with the **rented flat**, my savings and Deniz's depot job.
The only real question is **who buys the farm** when Graham retires at some point.
do: Keep doing the **morning milking** and calf rearing at Mill Lane Farm as normal.
Retake the **tractor test** I failed in spring and push the branch to sign the **pay deal**.
feel: **Relieved** and a little smug, because next year looks like this year.
S0.quote: The machines were never going to milk a cow better than Shona (her workmate).
fieldNote: She is secure on paper: **higher pay**, a rented flat and a partner in steady work.
The one worry she names is not AI but **Graham's age** and the farm's future owner.
She sees herself as the **opposite of office workers**, and enjoys that a little.

steps.text: Keep doing the morning milking and calf rearing at Mill Lane Farm
Push the union branch to sign the winter pay deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in the yard are years off and the union should be at the table before they come. I'd say it at the branch meeting and to anyone at the pub. Office people are the ones who should be worried in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've already seen the robot milkers at the Hendersons' place, two farms down. Graham went to look and came back quiet. The robot milking boxes at the Hendersons' farm do exactly what I do at five in the morning. I think Graham would put one in if the bank would lend him the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work, and I'd tell the union rep we need a rule that nobody loses their job when a farm brings in robots. I'd put a bit more aside each month too, maybe another hundred. I'm not going on any computer course, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, but I'd catch myself watching Graham's face when the machinery rep visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you see at the Hendersons' place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two red robot milking boxes, and the cows just walk in on their own when they want milking. Their lad who used to milk got moved onto fencing and tractor work. He says he likes it, but he doesn't look like he likes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you won't do a course. What happens if Graham buys one of those boxes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd fight it through the union first, and if that failed I'd go to another farm that still milks by hand. There are plenty of dairy farms within twenty miles. I know that's running from it, but that's what I'd do.

say: I'd say **robots in the yard** are years off, so office workers should worry first.
I'd tell the branch the **union** needs a seat at the table before any robot arrives.
think: I've seen the **robot milkers** at the Hendersons' and they do exactly my job.
Graham would buy one tomorrow if the **bank** would lend him the money.
do: Ask the union rep for a **no job losses** rule when farms bring in robots.
Put an extra **£100 a month** aside and refuse any computer course.
Move to **another dairy farm** that still milks by hand if Graham buys a robot.
feel: **Uneasy**, watching Graham's face whenever the **machinery rep** comes round.
S1.quote: The robot milking boxes at the Hendersons' farm do exactly what I do at five in the morning.
fieldNote: She's not worried about AI itself; she's worried about the **robot milking box** two farms down.
Her plan is to **resist through the union**, then move farms rather than learn new work.
She admits moving farms is **running from it**, which is honest for someone so set in her ways.

steps.text: Ask the union rep for a no-job-losses rule on farm robots
Put an extra £100 a month into savings
Move to a hand-milking dairy farm if Graham buys a robot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in, full stop. Tax the companies selling the robots and put the money into wages for people like me. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd say it loudly online, which I never usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the clever AI in 2028 doesn't touch me much, because Graham does the thinking on the farm. The robots in 2031 are the ones that get me. I'd be thirty-one, still not great at calving, and the robot is better at all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd save hard, and I'd sit down with Deniz and work out if we could live on his wage and the rent from the flat. I'd join the union's campaign and write to my MP for the first time in my life. When the robots come, I'd probably be out, and I don't know what I'd do then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like the floor's going. I can see 2031 coming and I don't have anything to do about it except shout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Deniz's wage and the flat. Could the two of you live on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about, if we stopped going away and sold my car. The flat brings in about six hundred a month. But Deniz fixes buses, and I'd bet the buses drive themselves by then too, so I don't trust that either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Three years between the clever AI and the robots. What would you do in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hold on, mostly. I'd keep milking, keep saving, and hope the union wins something. I know someone sensible would learn to run the robots, but I can't see myself doing that, and anyway they'd run themselves.

say: I'd say the **government** must tax the robot makers and protect farm wages.
I'd speak up at **every union meeting** and online, which I never usually do.
think: The thinking AI in 2028 barely touches me, because **Graham** does the farm's thinking.
The **robots in 2031** take my job, and I'd be thirty-one and still learning calving.
do: Save hard from **today** and work out a budget on **Deniz's wage** plus flat rent.
Join the **union campaign** and write to my **MP** for the first time.
Keep milking until the robots arrive, with **no clear plan** after that.
feel: **Sick**, like the floor is going and all I can do is **shout**.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-one, still not great at calving, and the robot is better at all of it.
fieldNote: She clearly separates **thinking AI** from robots and sees only the robots as her threat.
Her **flat and savings** give her runway, but no direction, and she knows it.
She dismisses learning to run robots **before trying**, which fits her dislike of new tech.
She now doubts even **Deniz's job**, so the household cushion feels thinner to her.

steps.text: Work out a budget on Deniz's wage and the flat rent
Write to the local MP about taxing farm robot makers
Join the union campaign to protect farm wages
Keep milking at Mill Lane Farm until robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: the union needs to get in early and get a deal. I'd say five years is enough time to write some proper rules if the politicians stop dithering. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is long enough that I can't pretend I didn't see it. Robots in 2034 means I'd be thirty-five. I'd have to do something with that time, and I hate that I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save, same as before, and I'd look at a job that robots can't do yet, maybe the cattle market or a milk tanker driver. Tanker driving needs a heavy goods licence, which is a lorry licence, so I'd have to pass a test. Honestly I'd probably put it off for two years and then panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a slow way. Like a bill you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You laughed when you said you'd put it off. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what I did with the tractor test. I knew for a year I needed it and I left it till Graham made me book it. I'd be the same with this, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Deniz about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Deniz (her partner) we should pay off the last of the flat's loan before 2034, so at least the flat is ours clean. Then if I'm out of work, we're not out of a home. That's the bit I'd actually do.

say: I'd say the **union** should get in early and win a deal before robots arrive.
I'd say **five years** is enough to write proper rules if politicians stop dithering.
think: Robots in **2034** mean I'd be thirty-five, and I can't pretend I didn't see it.
I'd probably **put off** acting for two years, the same way I did with the tractor test.
do: Pay off the **flat's loan** before 2034 so our home is safe.
Look at **milk tanker driving**, which needs a lorry licence and a test.
Keep saving and keep up the **union** pressure for a deal.
feel: **Anxious** in a slow way, like a bill I know is coming.
S3.quote: I'd tell Deniz (her partner) we should pay off the last of the flat's loan before 2034, so at least the flat is ours clean.
fieldNote: She's **self-aware** about putting things off, and uses the tractor test as proof.
The **flat** becomes her anchor; paying it off is the one step she's sure of.
Tanker driving is a **hands-on escape**, still exposed to robots, which she didn't notice.

steps.text: Pay off the flat's loan before 2034
Look into a lorry licence to drive milk tankers
Keep pressing the union branch for a robot deal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for the government to plan this properly, so there's no excuse. Farm workers should get paid retraining and a share of what the robots save. That's what I'd say at the branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels like forever and like nothing at the same time. Robots in 2039, I'd be nearly forty. That's a whole career gone, just as I'd finally be good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd keep milking for the first few years and not change much. I'd pay off the flat and keep saving. Somewhere around 2033 I'd look for something else, maybe with the council's grounds team or the cattle market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sharp. More of a dull ache. I'd still expect to lose the job, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd finally be good at it. What does being good at it look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calving a heifer on my own at three in the morning without ringing Shona (her workmate) is what being good at farming looks like. Knowing a cow's off her food before she's ill. I'm maybe halfway there, and by 2039 I'd be there, and then it wouldn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning anything new in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if the union ran it and it was about animals, not screens. A proper vet tech course, say. But not a computer thing, I'd be rubbish at it and I'd hate every minute.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves the government no excuse for not planning properly.
Farm workers should get **paid retraining** and a share of what the robots save.
think: By **2039** I'd be nearly forty, and a whole career would be gone.
I'd finally be **good at calving** right when it stopped mattering.
do: Keep milking at **Mill Lane Farm** for the first few years without big changes.
Pay off the **flat** and look for council or **cattle market** work around 2033.
feel: **Anxious** but duller than before, more of an **ache** than a jolt.
S4.quote: Calving a heifer on my own at three in the morning without ringing Shona (her workmate) is what being good at farming looks like.
fieldNote: Her **pride in skill** is the real loss for her, more than the money.
She'd consider a **vet tech course** only if the union runs it and it's hands-on.
Even with a decade, she plans to **wait** about seven years before moving.

steps.text: Keep milking at Mill Lane Farm for now
Pay off the flat and keep saving each month
Apply for council grounds or cattle market work around 2033

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Robots on the farm by 2031 and me with nothing else I know how to do. What would help is the union having a proper deal ready: notice, pay while you retrain, and something with animals at the end of it, not a screen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's making money from all this. It's not Graham and it's not me, it's whoever sells the robots. Farm work has always been hard, but at least the money stayed on the farm.

headlineQuote: Farm work has always been hard, but at least the money stayed on the farm.
portrait: Bianca, 27, is a junior **dairy hand** at Mill Lane Farm, milking ninety Friesians and rearing calves.
She has a **rented-out flat**, solid savings and a partner, Deniz, who mends buses.
She **avoids new technology** and would sooner move farms or fight through the union than retrain.
She is calm when AI flops but grows **alarmed** as robots for hands-on work come closer.
She blames the **robot sellers**, not her boss, for taking the money off the farm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with farm robots by 2031 and no other skill she trusts.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** with notice, paid retraining and **animal work** at the end, not screens.
